mappings.note: Names a repeating natural event, such as sunrise, that timekeeping was founded on: the basis of the process.
Names the sundial from its use of a moving shadow, a device identified by how it works.
Names an hourglass or candle clock as an ancient clock not using water, again device identification.
Names the bob of a simple pendulum.
Names the mean position, the rest point of the pendulum: a feature of the set-up rather than a description of the motion.
Names the pendulum's motion as oscillatory or periodic, which describes the phenomenon.
Names the time period, the quantity LO-104 names for the simple pendulum.
Whether the period depends on the bob's mass: the quantity tested against a variable that turns out not to govern it.
Length as the property that sets the period, the variable that does govern it.
The second as the SI unit of time.
Sixty seconds in a minute, a conversion used throughout the chapter's sums.
Sixty minutes in an hour, the companion conversion.
Names speed as distance covered in unit time.
States the speed formula.
Metre per second as the SI unit of speed.
The speedometer as the instrument that reads speed.
The odometer as the instrument that totals distance.

This row is misaligned: the stem repeats the odometer question while the printed answer is the cyclist calculation, distance equals speed times time. Both halves are measurement of distance and speed, so LO-104 is right either way; the mismatch itself is reported as a defect.
Defines average speed and says why it is used in place of a single speed: about the quantity and how it is computed.
Uniform against non-uniform linear motion, a distinction between kinds of motion.
Asks for one example of each kind from daily life, so the concept is being matched to lived experience rather than defined.
How equal distances in equal times identify uniform motion: applying the definition to an observation.
What a speedometer reads and in what units: the instrument and the unit of the quantity.
What an odometer reads and in what units, the companion instrument item.
Why the pendulum clock was a breakthrough in timekeeping: the historical significance of the invention.
How atomic and quartz clocks reach their accuracy through very rapid, stable vibrations: the working principle explained.
Sets up the pendulum and states the precautions (LO-100) and then determines the time period from timed oscillations (LO-104). Both are named in the question.
Defines both kinds of linear motion and then reads the two train tables to place each: classification of motion, with no speed computed.
What speedometer and odometer show at different stages, and how to get the average speed for the whole trip from them: measurement and calculation.
The path from sundials and water clocks to atomic clocks, and what drove the demand for accuracy: the history of the science.
Sprint speed in two units and then the time for a kilometre at that speed: three calculations in one item.
Why total distance over total time is enough for average speed even when the speed varied: the meaning of the calculated quantity.
Judges the motion from the interval distances and then computes the average speed over one hundred seconds; the calculation carries the marks.
Why Galileo's finding mattered for clockmaking (LO-108) rests on the period being set by length and not by amplitude or mass (LO-101). Both are needed for the answer.
Why standard units such as the second and the metre per second matter: about the units in which quantities are measured and reported.
Why the bowl clock cannot match a quartz watch, given a hole that may widen and a flow that varies: accuracy traced to the mechanism. Not LO-107, because the device is judged rather than built.
Odometer difference, total time and average speed, then whether that figure matches the speed while moving: a calculation and its interpretation.
A lighter bob of the same size would not change the time for ten oscillations: the period tested against mass again.
Split times over four fifty-metre stretches and then the average speed for the full two hundred metres: calculation throughout.
Whether three hours at a nominal eighty kilometres an hour really gives 240 km: the limits of a distance calculation when the speed is not steady.
Matching item covering the bob, one oscillation and the fact that the period is set by length: the motion described (LO-102) and the period tied to its governing variable (LO-101).
Matches the SI units of time, distance and speed and the formula for time taken: all measurement and calculation.
Matches the two kinds of linear motion (LO-102) with the speedometer and odometer (LO-104), so both strands are assessed in one item.
